title: Gaussian YOLOv3: An Accurate and Fast Object Detector Using Localization Uncertainty for Autonomous Driving
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: For autonomous driving, detectors must be both accurate and real time, yet one-stage detectors trade accuracy for speed while prior uncertainty-aware methods are either not real time, not applied to detection, or never used in the detection decision; conventional detectors output deterministic box coordinates with no uncertainty, so they cannot avoid false positives caused by mislocalization.
statements: Conventional detectors output deterministic bbox coordinates without uncertainty information, so they cannot prevent mislocalizations (false positives).
A false positive in autonomous driving can cause unexpected braking and fatal accidents.
Two-stage detectors are accurate but too slow, while one-stage detectors are fast but less accurate; previous accuracy-oriented schemes could not reach 30 fps at 512x512 or higher input.
Prior uncertainty methods (Kendall et al., Feng et al.) only predict an uncertainty level and do not utilize it in actual applications.
He et al.'s detection uncertainty method targets a two-stage detector, so it cannot support real-time operation.

evidence.quote: whereas the bbox coordinates (i.e., localization) of the detected object are known, the uncertainty of the bbox result is not.
Thus, conventional object detectors cannot prevent mislocalizations (i.e., FPs) because they output the deterministic results of the bbox without information regarding the uncertainty.
previous studies [1, 11, 29, 28] have been unable to meet a real-time detection speed of above 30 fps, which is a prerequisite for self-driving applications.
However, the methods proposed by Kendall et al. [12] and Feng et al. [6] only predict the level of uncertainty, and do not utilize this factor in actual applications.

background.summary: The paper builds on YOLO/YOLOv2/YOLOv3 one-stage detection, FPN-style multi-scale prediction inside YOLOv3, and Bayesian uncertainty modeling (Kendall & Gal) as adapted by prior driving-perception work; the gap claimed is that existing uncertainty methods do not feed into detection decisions and are incompatible with real-time one-stage detection.

However, in general, it still has a lower accuracy than a two-stage detector using a region proposal stage.
However, owing to the processing of the grid unit, localization errors are large and the detection accuracy is low, and thus it is unsuitable for autonomous driving applications.

solution.summary: Gaussian YOLOv3 models each of the four bbox coordinates in YOLOv3's detection layer as a Gaussian (mean and variance), replaces the squared-error box loss with a heteroscedastic negative log-likelihood loss that down-weights noisy targets, and multiplies the objectness and class scores by (1 - average localization uncertainty) at detection time to filter poorly localized boxes.
solution.approach: Emit mean and variance for every bbox coordinate, train with an NLL loss that attenuates inconsistent data, and use the predicted uncertainty as an extra score factor during detection.
components: Gaussian parameters (mu, Sigma) for tx, ty, tw, th at each predicted box
sigmoid preprocessing of means and variances in the detection layer
negative log-likelihood bbox loss with scale weighting and eps = 1e-9
loss attenuation that makes training robust to noisy data
detection criterion Cr = sigmoid(object) * sigmoid(class_i) * (1 - uncertainty_avg)
k-means clustered anchor priors per dataset

evidence.quote: the uncertainty of bbox can be modeled using each single Gaussian model of tx , ty , tw , and th .
the loss function of bbox is redesigned as a negative log likelihood (NLL) loss, whereas the loss function for objectness and class is not changed.
bbox with high uncertainty among the predicted results is filtered through the detection process.
Cr. = σ(Object) × σ(Classi ) × (1 − U ncertaintyaver ).
the redesigned loss function of bbox makes the model more robust to noisy data [12].

experiments.summary: The method is evaluated on the KITTI and BDD autonomous-driving datasets (plus COCO) against two-stage and one-stage detectors, measuring mAP and fps at matched input resolutions, validating that predicted uncertainty anti-correlates with IoU, and counting false positives and true positives against ground truth.

evidence.quote: The mAP of the proposed algorithm, Gaussian YOLOv3, improves by 3.09 compared to that of YOLOv3, and the detection speed is 43.13 fps, which enables real-time detection with a slight difference from YOLOv3.
Gaussian YOLOv3 improves the mAP by 3.5 compared with YOLOv3, and the detection speed is 42.5 fps, which is almost the same as YOLOv3.
For the KITTI and BDD validation sets, Gaussian YOLOv3 reduces the FP by 41.40% and 40.62%, respectively, compared to YOLOv3.
the IOU value tends to increase as the localization uncertainty decreases in both datasets.

limitations.summary: Accuracy at the standard 512x512 input still trails the most accurate prior method (SINet) on KITTI, there is a small fps drop relative to plain YOLOv3, only bbox localization uncertainty is modeled (not objectness or class uncertainty), and anchors must be re-clustered per dataset.
items: At 512x512 on KITTI the mAP is 1.81 below SINet, which is 1.8 times faster.
Detection speed drops slightly versus the baseline (43.13 vs 43.57 fps on KITTI; 42.5 vs 42.9 fps on BDD).
Only the bbox coordinates are modeled as Gaussians; objectness and class scores remain deterministic.
Anchor priors are dataset-specific, obtained by k-means clustering on each training set.

evidence.quote: although the mAP of Gaussian YOLOv3 with a 512 × 512 resolution is 1.81 lower than that of SINet [11]
Single Gaussian modeling for predicting the uncertainty of bbox only applies to the bbox coordinates of the YOLOv3 detection layer shown in Figure 1a.
The anchor size is extracted using k-means clustering for each training set of KITTI and BDD.

futureDirections.direction: Deploy the improved camera-based detection system to broaden the use of autonomous driving applications.
futureDirections.quote: the proposed algorithm can significantly improve the camera-based object detection system for autonomous driving, and is consequently expected to contribute significantly to the wide use of autonomous driving applications.

equations.name: NLL bbox loss
equations.expr: Lx = -sum gamma_ijk * log(N(x_G | mu_tx, Sigma_tx) + eps)

applications.detail: The detector is designed and evaluated for self-driving perception on the KITTI and BDD driving datasets, detecting cars, pedestrians, cyclists and traffic elements in real time.
applications.quote: must accurately detect cars, pedestrians, traffic signs, traffic lights, etc. in real time to ensure safe and correct control decisions [25].

applications.detail: False-positive reduction is tied directly to avoiding unexpected braking and fatal accidents in production vehicles.
applications.quote: the reduction in the FP prevents unnecessary unexpected braking, and the increase in the TP prevents fatal accidents from object detection errors.

deploymentClaims: Real-time detection at over 42 fps with 512x512 input despite the accuracy gains
Only 0.04% extra FLOPs (99.04e9 vs 99e9) from the Gaussian modeling of the output layer
Measured on an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and cuDNN v7

evidence.quote: the additional computation cost is negligible, and the proposed algorithm consequently maintains the real-time detection speed of over 42 fps with an input resolution of 512 × 512 despite the significant improvements in performance.
The experiment is conducted on an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and cuDNN v7.
